content_html_sanitized:
Posted July 23, 2001
See
As More and More Countries Begin to Question Cannabis Prohibition, The Debate Should Be An International. Basic Rights Versus Toothless Treaties. Analysis by Richard Cowan
(MarijuanaNews note: The UK now joins Canada and New Zealand in having formal parliamentary debates on prohibition. While these countries will naturally carry on their own national debates about their own laws in the context of their own environment, it would be absurd for them to pretend that their debates are unique and taking place in a vacuum.

It is shameful that DEAland is not joining in. After all, The Declaration of Independence referred to having " a decent Respect to the Opinions of Mankind " – but those words were written by a hemp farmer.)

The inquiry will ensure that the debate about drugs, sparked off by Michael Portillo's campaign for the Tory leadership, will be high on the political agenda for the next 12 months.
(MarijuanaNews note: Actually, that is giving Portillo too much credit. Others have done far more to advance the issue.)
See
The Accelerating Disintegration of Marijuana Prohibition in Europe. If the Tories Are " all about sex, drugs and rock'n'roll, " Where Can the Left Go? Embarrassment for Swedes. Dutch PM for Dinner.

Mr Blunkett appeared to be slapped down by No 10 after calling for an " adult debate " – seen as a hint that the Brixton policing experiment not to prosecute cannabis-users could herald a shift of policy towards decriminalisation. Mr Blair's official spokesman insisted there would be no change of approach on drugs.
See
A Weird Week in the World of Marijuana Prohibition: Paranoid in Boise, Practical in London, And an Unusual Line-Up On the Supreme Court. Two Stories and Two Footnotes.

The select committee will also investigate the consequences of the legal bans on drugs such as cocaine, ecstasy and heroin.
(MarijuanaNews note: If they are examining hard drugs policies, then legalizing cannabis will seem very moderate.)
